title: Frictionless onboard runway — notebook
content:
Goal: make first-10-mins experience for new customers (esp. Dedicated/Private) feel 'instant' and low-friction. Reduce time-to-value and reduce support handoffs for early integration.

Problem / signals:
- New Dedicated/private customers often hit two blockers: perceived latency on first requests (cold KV/cache + model cold start) and uncertainty about config choices (batching/quantization/replicas).
- Early tickets: onboarding > account setup > "why are my responses slow first 5 minutes?" and "what should I set for batch window?"
- Sales/professional services time cost high during first 2 weeks; opportunity to self-serve more.

Hypothesis: a small set of UX + runtime defaults + automated warmup flows (= "onboard runway") will reduce first-week support volume by 30% and improve time-to-first-successful-call metric by >=50%.

Target users:
- Platform/infra engineers integrating Redwood Dedicated into backend flows
- Solutions engineers testing Private deployments in staging
- Product teams evaluating performance for critical user journeys

Success metrics (provisional):
- Time-to-first-successful-call (median) for new private/dedicated projects drops from X to ~50% of baseline
- Support ticket volume tagged "initial-performance" down 30% in first 14 days
- % of customers that finish guided runbook within 1 hour — target 60%+
- NPS-ish: onboarding satisfaction survey score > 4/5 within 30 days

Core components (MVP):
1) Guided "Runway" wizard in Console
   - minimal questions: primary use-case (chat/batch/embeddings), target p99 latency budget, expected QPS
   - outputs: recommended model family, quantization tier (if available), batch window suggestions, KV cache warm/retain policy
   - shows estimated cost delta between recommended configs
2) Automated warmers + staged warmup policy
   - small synthetic workload runner that (optionally) sends safe, non-PHI warmup prompts to prepopulate KV caches and JIT kernels
   - three-stage: cold-start probe -> light warmup -> steady-state rehearsal
   - knobs: concurrency, sequence length distribution, affinity to real prompt types (dev can upload 3 sample prompts)
3) One-click prescriptive config for Dedicated
   - apply recommended batch settings and a warmup schedule to pool during onboarding
   - optionally reserve short burst capacity (10–15m) for ramping tests
4) Quickstart template library
   - 3-4 tiny example apps (chat, summarization, reranking) with config + sample prompts + perf dashboard links
5) Observability hooks
   - pre-populated dashboard template showing warmup status, per-token latency, cold-start events, KV hit rate
   - telemetry schema and early signals for ops/troubleshooting

User flows (sketch):
- New Dedicated customer creates a project -> Console prompts: "Run onboarding runway?" -> choose guided or manual
- Guided flow: answer 3 questions -> upload up to 3 canonical prompts (optional) -> Runway estimates config -> approve
- System schedules warmup job for next 10–30 minutes, shows live progress and simulated QPS metrics; recommended config applied if approved
- After run, Console shows before/after median latency and cost delta, with ability to roll back

Rough user stories (for backlog):
- As an infra engineer, I want a guided onboarding wizard so I can quickly apply safe defaults and avoid guessing batch windows.
- As an SE, I want to upload 3 representative prompts so the warmup job exercises realistic token lengths and KV usage.
- As an ops lead, I want a prepopulated dashboard that highlights cold-start events during first 24 hours.
- As a product manager, I want the wizard to estimate cost impact of warming vs not warming (ballpark numbers).

Experiment ideas / A/B
- A/B wizard vs no-wizard: track time-to-first-successful-call and support ticket creation
- Warmup intensity: light vs aggressive — measure cost vs latency improvement curve
- Prepopulated prompts vs user-supplied: does user-supplied dramatically improve warmup efficiency?

Telemetry + instrumentation
- New metrics: warmup_job_id, warmup_stage, kv_hit_rate_during_warmup, kernel_compile_events, cold_start_count
- Tag events with project_id + customer_tier so we can analyze Dedicated vs Private behavior
- Retention: keep warmup traces for 7 days with aggregated histograms

Risks / constraints
- Privacy: cannot send customer PHI to generic warmup corpora. Must either only run warmup with user-supplied prompts or synthetic safe templates. Legal/security review required for default synthetic prompts.
- Cost: warmup jobs cost money. Need explicit opt-in for auto-warm within billing period or allow sales credits to cover.
- HW compatibility: some model variants may not support fast warmup (quantized kernels). Need failover path: "no warmup recommended" and clear messaging.

Open questions
- Should warmup be opt-in or opt-out for Private installs? (Security teams may prefer opt-in.)
- How often to run warmup after first day? periodic, weekly, or only on deploys? Propose: on model rollouts and weekly for active projects.
- How to quantify "successful" warmup? KV hit rate threshold? p95 latency improvement?
- API vs Console: should we provide an onboarding-runway API for infra-as-code customers? (Yes, likely.)

Next actions (short-term)
- Spike: build a minimal warmup runner that accepts 1 prompt and 1 concurrency knob -> measure p95 improvement (owner: Ravi) [1 week]
- Console mock: three-step wizard mockups and copy (owner: Marta) [1 week]
- Legal/sales sync: confirm billing/PHI constraints (owner: Sam) [2 weeks]
- Add JIRA ticket template: JIRA-PI-879 (linked)

Notes / references
- Related: "first-run-warmup-flow-prd-journal.json" in users/ (concept overlap) — but this doc focuses on a guided UX + safe defaults + cost estimators.
- Slack threads: #se-onboarding, #dedicated-ops

Random thoughts (brain dump):
- Could surface a "warmup credit" promo for new Dedicated trials (3 hours burst) to encourage self-testing.
- Consider an internal "warmup lab" runbook for SEs to reproduce customer issues — reproducible via shareable warmup_job_id.
- If user uploads proprietary prompts, offer a redacted preview and legal checkbox before running on hosted infra.

Status: rough sketch. Want to keep this lightweight — next step is spike + mock + legal check.
